# `nish/net/quic-listener`

What a QUIC version 1 server answers to a datagram no connection owns: Version Negotiation for a version it does not speak (RFC 9000 §6, §17.2.1), a Retry that asks a client to prove its address before any connection state exists (§8.1.2, §17.2.5), and a stateless reset for a packet sent to a connection the server no longer has (§10.3). Sans-IO, like the rest of `nish/net`, and stateless in the sense the RFC means: nothing it answers depends on any connection.

```ts
import {
  QUIC_LISTENER_ANSWER_SIZE,
  QUIC_LISTENER_ENTROPY_SIZE,
  QUIC_LISTENER_FLIGHT_MAX,
  QUIC_LISTENER_FLIGHT_QUANTUM,
  QUIC_LISTENER_MAX_TOKEN_LIFETIME,
  QUIC_LISTENER_MIN_RESET,
  QUIC_LISTENER_RESET_BURST,
  QUIC_LISTENER_RESET_INTERVAL,
  QUIC_LISTEN_ACCEPT,
  QUIC_LISTEN_DROP,
  QUIC_LISTEN_INVALID_TOKEN,
  QUIC_LISTEN_RETRY,
  QUIC_LISTEN_STATELESS_RESET,
  QUIC_LISTEN_VERSION_NEGOTIATION,
  QuicFlight,
  QuicListener,
  QuicListenerAnswer,
  quicListenerFlightTime,
  quicListenerPaceTime,
  quicListenerReceiveSegments,
  quicListenerTakeFlight,
  quicListenerTakePaced,
} from "nish/net/quic-listener";
```

```ts
import { QuicListener, QuicListenerAnswer, QUIC_LISTEN_ACCEPT, QUIC_LISTENER_ANSWER_SIZE } from "nish/net/quic-listener";
import { QuicConnection } from "nish/net/quic";

const listener = new QuicListener(config, entropy);      // entropy: QUIC_LISTENER_ENTROPY_SIZE random bytes
const answer = new QuicListenerAnswer(QUIC_LISTENER_ANSWER_SIZE);  // once, beside the listener
// For a datagram buf[at .. at + len) whose first packet no connection owns:
if (listener.handleWindow(buf, at, len, fromAddress, now, answer) === QUIC_LISTEN_ACCEPT) {
  const conn = new QuicConnection(config, connectionEntropy);
  if (answer.retried) { conn.acceptRetry(answer.originalDcid, answer.retryScid); }
  conn.receiveWindow(buf, at, len, now);
} else if (toI32(answer.reply.length) > 0) {
  … send answer.reply back to fromAddress …
}
```

<scalar-callout type="info">

**Nothing is kept per datagram** (H3-3 in `docs/security/http3.md`).
`handleWindow` reads the datagram where it lies, its header parsed in
place, and writes every answer into the caller's `QuicListenerAnswer`,
whose arrays were given their room once; every MAC, key and seal is
computed in scratch the listener made at start-up. `handle` is the same
over a whole array, into an answer of its own each time, for a caller
that keeps them.

</scalar-callout>

<scalar-detail title="Routing is the caller's">

The listener sees only datagrams the caller
could not hand to a live connection, and it must see only those: a stateless
reset carries the token for the packet's connection ID, and handing the
listener a packet for a connection that is still alive would give that
token, which ends the connection, to whoever sent it (RFC 9000 §21.11).

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Retry tokens">

**Retry tokens** (§8.1.4). They are this server's own format: a marker byte, the
time the token was issued, and the client's original Destination
Connection ID, then 16 bytes of HMAC-SHA256 under the configuration's
`retryTokenKey` over all of that, the Retry's Source Connection ID (which
the client's next Initial must be sent to) and the client's address as the
caller gives it, port included. So a token is good only from the address
it was sent to, only for the connection it was issued for, and only for
`retryTokenLifetime` milliseconds. A token that carries the marker and fails
any of that is an invalid Retry token, which closes the attempt with
INVALID_TOKEN (§8.1.2); a token without the marker, which some other
server issued, is treated as no token at all (§8.1.3).

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Stateless resets">

**Stateless resets** (§10.3). They end in the token `quicStatelessResetToken`
derives (computed in place, by `quicConnResetTokenInto`) from the configuration's static key and the packet's connection
ID, so a server that restarted with the same key can end the connections
it lost. RFC 9000 §10.3 and §10.3.3 bound them, and each bound is held
here. A reset is sent only for a short header, and is always shorter than
the datagram that caused it, so two endpoints resetting each other shrink
to nothing; one byte shorter for a datagram of 43 bytes or fewer, and
never under 21 bytes, so a datagram of 21 or fewer gets none. That also
bounds amplification at less than one to one. They are rate limited:
`QUIC_LISTENER_RESET_BURST` at once, then one per
`QUIC_LISTENER_RESET_INTERVAL` milliseconds. Each reset's other bytes are
unpredictable, from the listener's own generator.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Pacing">

**Pacing** (RFC 9002 §7.7). It is the carrier's send loop, so it is here
beside the rest of what the carrier calls: `quicListenerTakePaced` takes a
connection's next datagram only when its pacer has the credit for it, and
`quicListenerPaceTime` says when it will. The pacer earns 5/4 of the
congestion window per smoothed RTT and lets a burst of at most the initial
window go at once, so a flight leaves spread over the round trip instead
of in one burst that overruns a queue on the path.

```text
let out: u8[] | null = quicListenerTakePaced(conn, now);
while (out !== null) { … send it with conn.datagramEcn … ; out = quicListenerTakePaced(conn, now); }
… and wake at the earlier of conn.deadline() and quicListenerPaceTime(conn, now)
```

</scalar-detail>

A carrier that sends whole flights with `quicListenerTakeFlight`, below,
wakes at `quicListenerFlightTime` instead, as `Http3Server` does: a flight
waits for more credit than one datagram, so the pace time can come first.

<scalar-detail title="GSO and GRO">

**GSO and GRO** (`nish:net`'s `UDP_SEGMENT` and `UDP_GRO`). A carrier that
sends with segmentation offload takes a whole flight at once:
`quicListenerTakeFlight` writes as many datagrams as the pacer has credit
for back to back into one buffer, every one `QUIC_CONN_DATAGRAM_SIZE`
bytes but the last, which is what one `udpSendTo` with that segment size
cuts back into datagrams; each is written in place, so a flight allocates
nothing. The flight is paced as a whole: it is as long as the pacer's
credit, and charged to it datagram by datagram, so a burst is never more
than the initial window however the carrier sends it. It starts only on a
millisecond's earning, up to four datagrams, so a fast connection's pacer,
which earns by the microsecond, does not let it out a datagram per send;
`quicListenerFlightTime` says when. On the receiving
side, `quicListenerReceiveSegments` hands a connection the datagrams of
one GRO receive, segment by segment, in place.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="ECN">

**ECN** (RFC 9000 §13.4). A carrier whose platform sends the ECN bits it
is given sets the connection's `ecnMarking` and sends each datagram with
the codepoint the connection marked it with: `conn.datagramEcn` after a
`takeDatagramInto` or `quicListenerTakePaced`, `flight.ecn` for a flight.
One send carries one codepoint, so a flight ends before a datagram the
connection would mark otherwise. The listener's own answers go unmarked.

```ts
const flight = new QuicFlight();
const n: i32 = quicListenerTakeFlight(conn, now, buf, 0, toI32(buf.length), flight);
if (n > 0) { udpSendTo(fd, buf, 0, n, peer, flight.count > 1 ? flight.segment : 0, flight.ecn); }
```

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Sans-IO and deterministic">

The caller gives the time, the client's
address and, once, `QUIC_LISTENER_ENTROPY_SIZE` random bytes: every
unpredictable byte the listener sends (a Retry's connection ID and unused
bits, Version Negotiation's unused bits, a reset's padding and length) is
HMAC-SHA256 under that seed of a counter. So a recorded exchange replays
byte for byte.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Secrets">

The seed lives in the listener and the static keys in the
`QuicServerConfig`, for the server's lifetime, as plain bytes, since a
`Secret` may not be a field (NL2430). `release()` wipes the listener's own,
and `Http3Server.stop` the configuration's with them; QUIC-5 in
`docs/security/quic.md` records what is left.

</scalar-detail>

Written from RFC 9000, in this module's own structure; nothing here is
ported from another implementation. Private names carry the
`quicListener` prefix (`docs/wp26-stdlib.md` §3e).

## quicListenerReceiveSegments

Hands `conn` the datagrams of one receive, `buf[off .. off + len)`, at
`now`: one datagram when `segment` is 0, else a GRO receive cut every
`segment` bytes (the last may be shorter). Each is read in place. Answers
how many it handed over.

```ts
function quicListenerReceiveSegments(
  conn: QuicConnection,
  buf: u8[],
  off: i32,
  len: i32,
  segment: i32,
  now: i64,
): i32
```

#### Parameters

<scalar-field name="conn" type="QuicConnection" required>

The connection the datagrams belong to.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="buf" type="u8[]" required>

The receive buffer; read, not kept.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="off" type="i32" required>

The index in `buf` of the first byte received.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="len" type="i32" required>

The bytes received.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="segment" type="i32" required>

The GRO segment size in bytes, or 0 (or less) for a single datagram.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="now" type="i64" required>

The caller's time in milliseconds.

</scalar-field>

#### Returns

<scalar-field name="returns" type="i32">

How many datagrams were handed over: always 1 when `segment` is 0 or less, whatever `len`;
  otherwise one per `segment` bytes of `len`, rounded up, which is 0 when `len` is 0 or less.

</scalar-field>

## quicListenerTakeFlight

Writes the next flight `conn` sends at `now` into `buf[at .. at + cap)`,
datagram after datagram, for one GSO send, and answers its length in
bytes (0 for none); `flight` says how many datagrams it holds and the
segment size. A flight starts only once the pacer has the credit
`quicListenerFlightTime` waits for, a millisecond's earning of one to four
datagrams; then each datagram goes only when the pacer has credit for a
full one (RFC 9002 §7.7) and is charged at its real size, as
`quicListenerTakePaced` does, so the flight is the pacer's whole credit
and no more. It stops at the first datagram shorter than
`QUIC_CONN_DATAGRAM_SIZE`, which can only be the last of a segmented send,
at `QUIC_LISTENER_FLIGHT_MAX` datagrams, when `cap` has no room for
another, and before a datagram whose ECN codepoint would not be the first's.

```ts
function quicListenerTakeFlight(
  conn: QuicConnection,
  now: i64,
  buf: u8[],
  at: i32,
  cap: i32,
  flight: QuicFlight,
): i32
```

#### Parameters

<scalar-field name="conn" type="QuicConnection" required>

The connection to send for.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="now" type="i64" required>

The caller's time in milliseconds.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="buf" type="u8[]" required>

Where the flight is written.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="at" type="i32" required>

The index in `buf` of the flight's first byte.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="cap" type="i32" required>

The bytes of `buf` from `at` the flight may use; under `QUIC_CONN_DATAGRAM_SIZE` sends nothing.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="flight" type="QuicFlight" required>

Overwritten with the flight's datagram count, segment size and ECN codepoint; all 0
  when nothing was written.

</scalar-field>

#### Returns

<scalar-field name="returns" type="i32">

The flight's length in bytes, or 0 when the pacer holds it back or nothing is due.

</scalar-field>

## quicListenerTakePaced

The next datagram `conn` sends at `now`, as `takeDatagram` answers it,
but only when the connection's pacer has the credit for a full datagram
(RFC 9002 §7.7); `null` when it has not, or when nothing is due. The
datagram is charged to the pacer at its real size.

```ts
function quicListenerTakePaced(
  conn: QuicConnection,
  now: i64,
): u8[] | null
```

#### Parameters

<scalar-field name="conn" type="QuicConnection" required>

The connection to send for.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="now" type="i64" required>

The caller's time in milliseconds.

</scalar-field>

#### Returns

<scalar-field name="returns" type="u8[] | null">

A new datagram to send, the caller's; or `null` when the pacer holds it back or nothing is due.

</scalar-field>

## QuicListener

The server's answers to datagrams no connection owns, under one
`QuicServerConfig`. Make one when the server starts, with the same
configuration its connections use, and hand it every such datagram with
the address it came from and the time.

A configuration whose `statelessResetKey` or `retryTokenKey` is not
`QUIC_CONN_STATIC_KEY_SIZE` bytes, or whose `retryTokenLifetime` is outside
1 to `QUIC_LISTENER_MAX_TOKEN_LIFETIME`, or entropy of another length, make
a listener that drops everything.

Everything an answer is computed in is made here, once: the header a
datagram is parsed into, the HMAC and HKDF scratch, the Initial secrets
and key slots of the INVALID_TOKEN close, and the generator's block. So
`handleWindow` reads the datagram where it lies and keeps nothing.

```ts
class QuicListener
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new QuicListener(config: QuicServerConfig, entropy: u8[])` | A listener under `config`; `entropy`'s `QUIC_LISTENER_ENTROPY_SIZE` bytes are copied, then wiped in the caller's array. |
| `initialClient: u8[]` | The Initial secrets of an INVALID_TOKEN close, and its keys, both directions. |
| `initialServer: u8[]` |  |
| `kdf: HkdfScratch` | Every HMAC and HKDF the listener computes runs here; its `sha256` makes tokens, resets and the generator's blocks. |
| `pool: u8[]` | Unpredictable bytes not yet used, from `poolHead`, and the counter the next block is made from. |
| `poolHead: i32` |  |
| `readSlot: QuicKeysSlot` |  |
| `resetsLimited: i32` |  |
| `resetsSent: i32` | Stateless resets sent, and ones the rate limit held back. |
| `seed: u8[]` |  |
| `spare: QuicListenerAnswer` | What `handle` answers into before it copies the answer out. |
| `tag: u8[]` | A full HMAC-SHA256 tag, wiped once its 16 bytes are used. |
| `writeSlot: QuicKeysSlot` |  |
| `handle(datagram: u8[], address: u8[], now: i64): QuicListenerAnswer` | `handleWindow` over the whole of `datagram`, into an answer of its own, made with exactly the room its reply takes: for a caller that keeps each answer, at the cost of one `QuicListenerAnswer` a datagram. A carrier makes one answer and calls `handleWindow`. |
| `handleWindow(datagram: u8[], at: i32, len: i32, address: u8[], now: i64, answer: QuicListenerAnswer): i32` | Decides what to answer a datagram whose first packet no connection owns, `datagram[at .. at + len)`, read where it lies, from `address` (the client's address as the caller's socket reports it, port included) at `now` (the caller's monotonic time in milliseconds), into `answer`, whose arrays are refilled in their own room. Answers `answer.kind`. See the module header for the rules; nothing a peer sends makes it panic, and nothing it does keeps arena memory. A window outside `datagram` is the caller's mistake, and panics. |
| `release(): void` | Ends the listener: wipes the seed and the generator's unused bytes, the tag and the HMAC and HKDF scratch, the INVALID_TOKEN close's Initial secrets and key slots, and `handle`'s spare answer, which holds the last one; `handle` and `handleWindow` then drop every datagram they are handed. The other methods still run, under the zeroed seed, and are the caller's not to call. What `handle` returned is the caller's to wipe. The configuration's keys are not the listener's to wipe: `Http3Server.stop` wipes them with the rest of the server. |

## QuicListenerAnswer

What `QuicListener.handleWindow` decided about one datagram: `kind` is a
`QUIC_LISTEN_*`, and `reply` the datagram to send back, empty when there
is none. For `QUIC_LISTEN_ACCEPT` after a Retry, `retried` is set and
`originalDcid` and `retryScid` are what `QuicConnection.acceptRetry` takes.

Make one once, with `QUIC_LISTENER_ANSWER_SIZE` as its `room`, and hand it
to every `handleWindow`: the constructor gives `reply` that room and each
ID 20 bytes, and each answer refills them in it, its length the answer's,
so answering allocates nothing (H3-3). A smaller room still works, and
grows the first time an answer needs more; `handle` makes each answer
with exactly the room its reply takes.

```ts
class QuicListenerAnswer
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new QuicListenerAnswer(room: i32)` | An empty answer with room for a reply of `room` bytes. |
| `kind: i32` |  |
| `originalDcid: u8[]` |  |
| `reply: u8[]` |  |
| `retried: boolean` |  |
| `retryScid: u8[]` |  |
| `wipe(): void` | Zeroes the last answer: `reply` across its whole room and each ID across its 20 bytes, so a Retry's token, a stateless reset's token and the IDs leave no copy beyond the arrays' lengths either. Each is left that long and all zero, `kind` a drop. An answer whose reply grew past its room keeps what lies beyond the longest length it is wiped at; one made with `QUIC_LISTENER_ANSWER_SIZE` never grows. The caller's to call once it has sent the answer `QuicListener.handle` gave, and before it drops it. |

## Limits

<scalar-grid cols="2">

<scalar-card title="QUIC_CONN_DATAGRAM_SIZE" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_LISTENER_ANSWER_SIZE: i32`

The largest answer the listener sends, and so the room `QuicListenerAnswer`
makes for `reply`: a stateless reset is at most a full datagram (RFC 9000
§10.3); a Version Negotiation packet, which echoes two IDs of up to 255
bytes, a Retry and the INVALID_TOKEN close are all shorter.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="64" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_LISTENER_FLIGHT_MAX: i32`

The most datagrams one GSO send carries: Linux's `UDP_MAX_SEGMENTS`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="4,800" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_LISTENER_FLIGHT_QUANTUM: i32`

The most credit a paced flight waits for before it starts: four datagrams.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="60,000" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_LISTENER_MAX_TOKEN_LIFETIME: i64`

The longest a Retry token may be accepted for, in milliseconds: a client returns one within a round trip.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="21" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_LISTENER_MIN_RESET: i32`

The smallest stateless reset (RFC 9000 §10.3): a first byte, at least 38
unpredictable bits after the fixed ones, and the 16-byte token.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="16" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_LISTENER_RESET_BURST: i32`

The most stateless resets the listener sends at once, before the rate limit applies.

</scalar-card>

</scalar-grid>

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="100" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_LISTENER_RESET_INTERVAL: i64`

After the burst, one stateless reset per this many milliseconds.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="1" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_LISTEN_ACCEPT: i32`

Make a connection and hand it the datagram; after a Retry, `acceptRetry` it first.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="0" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_LISTEN_DROP: i32`

Nothing to send and no connection to make: the datagram is dropped.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="4" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="3" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="5" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

Send `reply`, a stateless reset (§10.3).

<scalar-card title="2" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">
